newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.
newsitem.headline: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London closed slightly higher on late short-covering after an earlier round of arbitrage selling against New York fizzled out. Front month January closed $1 higher at $1,332 per tonne, while March added $13 to close at $1,275. News that Colombia, Ivory Coast and Uganda intend to tighten the ACPC retention scheme had no immediate impact on prices. Brazilian sources already said that there is no need for a further cut in export allocations and traders in Brazil have already expressed their concern over any reduction in Brazil's 6 million bag quota.

In New York arabica futures closed sharply higher with the December contract still leading the way. December added 4.40 cents/lb to close at 123.40 cents/lb, while March closed 1.75 cents/lb higher at 109.85 cents/lb. Open interest remains stubbornly high for three days left before expiration and this was behind much of the rise today. Other months were dragged up, but gains were limited in comparison. While time has essentially run out for coffee to arrive and be delivered against December (notices were zero today), the spread action suggests coffee should become available against March, traders said. Given the hefty premium (13.55 cents/lb) for December, processors were content to stay on the sidelines until the month goes off the board next Wednesday.

Traders said roasters still need coffee but are not prepared to pay the high price. It was added that while prompt supplies remained tight, keeping spot differentials firm, the flow of coffee from Mexico and some Central American coffee- producing countries is expected to pick up in January.

VENEZUELA - Coffee production in 1996/97 (October/September) is forecast to fall to 958,300 bags, down from 1.265 million bags produced in 1995/96 and 1.1 million bags produced in 1994/95. The fall in production is ascribed to unseasonal rains over the past few weeks. However, production in 1997/98 is expected to recover to 1.5 million bags, due to the planting of 25,000 new hectares of coffee, an increase of more than 10 percent over 1996/97.

ECUADOR - According to trade sources, exports of green coffee in 1996/97 (April/March) are forecast to reach 1.4 million 60-kg bags, up from 1.317 million bags exported in 1995/96. Of the total expected to be exported in 1996/97 750,000 bags will be arabicas and 650,000 bags robustas compared to 681,689 and 634,893 bags respectively last year. Soluble exports in 1996/97 are put at 560,000 bags, up from 351,067 bags the previous year.

BRAZIL - Brazil's Espirito Santo state will produce 3.59 million 60-kg bags of coffee in 1997/98, down 27.69 per cent from 4.97 million bags in 1996/97, according to the first estimate from the state agricultural secretariat. Output of arabica coffee is expected to see the largest percentage drop of 37.17 per cent to 1.06 million bags from this year's 1.69 million bags. Conillon coffee production is forecast to drop 22.81 per cent to 2.53 million bags from a 1996/97 crop of 3.29 million bags.

SPAIN - Spain imported 263,649 bags of coffee in August 1996, 26 percent more in the same month the previous year. That brought total imports since the beginning of 1996 up to 2.385 million bags, 9.6 percent more than was imported the same period in 1995. Total imports in calendar year 1995 rose by 2.2 percent to 3.225 million bags. Main suppliers of green coffee in January/August 1996 were Uganda (646,900 vs 436,400 bags), Honduras (116,100 vs 74,800 bags), Brazil (189,300 vs 414,400 bags), Colombia (244,800 vs 213,800 bags) and Vietnam (134,700 vs 161,800 bags). The country exported 338,500 bags of coffee in January/August 1996, 26 percent more than was exported the same period in 1995. Total exports in calendar year 1995 dropped by 6.7 percent to 401,000 bags.
